fixes.explanation: Ziklag it is, friend. These first helpers come to David there while he's still banished from the presence of Saul, Israel's king (1 Chronicles 12:1). David is banished, and men come to him anyway. I'd call that a good sign.

Both hands, friend. The text says they're archers who can use the right hand and the left to sling stones and shoot arrows (1 Chronicles 12:2). That's what sets them apart. I've got one mustache for everything and I STILL drop the cookie box.

Spear, friend. These Gadites are experts with the shield and spear (1 Chronicles 12:8). That's a pair you can count on: one to block and one to thrust. Same as a good oven mitt and a hot pan, one protects while the other works.

A hundred, friend. The least of these Gadite commanders was a match for a hundred, and the greatest for a thousand (1 Chronicles 12:14). That's the LEAST of them. I can barely hold my own against one stubborn batch of dough.

Not quite. The text says they crossed the Jordan in the first month when it was overflowing all its banks (1 Chronicles 12:15). Low water wouldn't spill over its banks. That's a river with no room left.

False is right. These Gadites crossed the Jordan in the first month when it was overflowing all its banks (1 Chronicles 12:15). The river was over its banks, and they crossed it anyway. I get nervous when my timer gets loud.

That's what he says, friend. Amasai, chief of the Thirty, says, “We are yours, O David! We are with you, O son of Jesse!” (1 Chronicles 12:18). The Spirit came upon him, and his words are plain and definite. I wish I could sound that sure when someone asks if I want another cookie.

The raiders, friend. These Manasseh chiefs helped David against the raiders, for they were all mighty men of valor and commanders in the army (1 Chronicles 12:21). They defected to him when he went to Ziklag. Good help is a gift.

The Moabites don't appear in this verse. The text says these Manasseh chiefs helped David against the raiders (1 Chronicles 12:21). They were mighty men of valor and commanders in the army, and the raiders are who they helped him against.

The army of God. The text says men came to David day after day to help him, “…until he had a great army, like the army of God.” (1 Chronicles 12:22). It grew day after day, one arrival after another. That's how my own bakery got busy, one hungry baker at a time.

That's the reason. The text says these men came to David at Hebron to turn Saul's kingdom over to him (1 Chronicles 12:23). They came armed for battle, and they came for a purpose. A crowd with one purpose is a beautiful thing.

Not quite. The text says all the rest of the Israelites were of one mind to make David king (1 Chronicles 12:38). That's the opposite of divided. It's rare to get a whole nation to agree on anything. I can't even get a kitchen to agree on a topping.

True. The text says they spent three days eating and drinking with David, “…for their relatives had provided for them.” (1 Chronicles 12:39). Their relatives did the providing. That's a lot of supplies for three days.

It's true, actually. The text says they spent three days eating and drinking with David, “…for their relatives had provided for them.” (1 Chronicles 12:39). The supplies came from their relatives. Eating and drinking for three days is the picture the text gives.
Fear isn't how it ends. The passage closes with, “Indeed, there was joy in Israel.” (1 Chronicles 12:40). After the crowds, the food and the three days together, joy is where the passage lands.
